## What you will learn

- Explain all four H-bridge states in terms of where the motor's current *goes*, not just what the truth table says.
- Choose a PWM frequency from the motor's electrical time constant, and predict the current ripple it produces.
- Predict, with numbers, why drive/brake (slow decay) gives a linear duty-to-speed curve and drive/coast (fast decay) gives a huge deadband.
- Compute the DRV8874's current-regulation trip point, its losses and its junction temperature, and say when it will thermally shut down.
- Design the IPROPI → Pico ADC network — scaling, filtering, protection — and explain why a "normal" resistor divider silently disables the current limit.

## Why it matters

[01.08](../01-first-robot/01.08-first-motor-spin.md) made a wheel turn: PWM on two pins, a duty number, motion. That's enough to drive a robot around a room, and not enough to explain why the same duty gives a different speed after you change one line in `motors.py`, why the driver is too hot to touch after a carpet test, why the robot's velocity controller fights a deadband below 12 % duty, or why the encoder counts glitch on every reversal.

Everything in modules 08 (control) and 09 (odometry) sits on top of this layer. A PID controller that has to fight a non-linear driver is a PID controller you will tune three times. And every number here becomes a constraint later: the 2.95 A current limit caps the acceleration you can command, the thermal limit caps how long you can push a robot up a ramp, and the braking energy decides whether "stop now" is safe for the driver.

## Concept

An H-bridge is four switches around a motor. That part you know from [FE.12](../optional-foundations/electronics/FE.12-h-bridges-motor-drivers.md). The part that decides how your robot behaves is this: **a motor is an inductor, and an inductor does not let its current stop.**

When you open the switch that was feeding the motor, the current keeps flowing — it must, because energy is stored in the winding's magnetic field. It will find a path. Your only choice is *which* path you offer it:

- Offer it the two low-side switches (both motor terminals shorted to ground): the current circulates in a near-zero-resistance loop and decays **slowly**. This is **slow decay**, also called **brake**.
- Offer it nothing: the current is forced through the bridge's body diodes back into the battery, against the full supply voltage, and dies **fast**. This is **fast decay**, also called **coast**.
- Offer it nothing *and* the motor is still spinning: then the motor is a generator and the diodes deliver its energy into your power rail. That's how braking can push your 12.6 V bus to 34 V.

A .NET analogy that actually fits: PWM's "off" state is like a connection you are done with. You can return it to the pool (slow decay: cheap, the current stays in the loop) or tear it down and reopen it next time (fast decay: expensive, everything has to be rebuilt each period). Both work; one of them costs you 90 % of your low-speed range.

The second idea is that the driver is not a passive switch. The DRV8874 **measures its own output current** every PWM cycle and chops the duty when the current crosses a threshold you set with one resistor. It also hands you that current measurement on a pin. Used properly it is a free ammeter on every wheel; wired naively it either destroys a GPIO pin or quietly disables the protection you thought you had.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "Draw the current path through the DRV8874 for each of the four input combinations, and tell me which two of them have current flowing through a body diode."

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — The four states, as current paths

| IN1 | IN2 | OUT1 | OUT2 | Name | Where the winding current goes when it was flowing OUT1 → OUT2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | Hi-Z | Hi-Z | coast | out of OUT2 through the **low-side body diode**, back in through the **high-side body diode** of OUT1 — i.e. into the supply, against $V_M$ |
| 1 | 0 | $V_M$ | GND | drive forward | from the supply through the high-side FET, through the motor, out through the low-side FET |
| 0 | 1 | GND | $V_M$ | drive reverse | mirror image |
| 1 | 1 | GND | GND | brake | round and round through the two **low-side FETs**: the loop sees only $R_M + R_{DS}$ |

The two "stopped" rows are not the same thing at all. In brake, the loop voltage opposing the current is the motor's own back-EMF $E = k\omega$, typically a few volts. In coast, the loop voltage is $V_M + 2V_{SD} \approx 13.8$ V — twenty times larger, so the current dies twenty times faster and the average torque collapses.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** Both high-side and low-side FETs of the same leg on at once is a **shoot-through** short across the battery. The DRV8874 inserts about 100 ns of dead time to prevent it. This is the reason you never drive an H-bridge from two independent software timers with hand-rolled timing — use the PWM peripheral, as `motors.py` does.

### Level 2 — PWM frequency: the motor's electrical time constant

The winding is $L_M$ in series with $R_M$. Its electrical time constant is

$$\tau_e = \frac{L_M}{R_M + R_{DS(on)}}$$

**Example (karmel's Yahboom 520).** $R_M = 3.0\ \Omega$ from the stall current ([02.01](02.01-datasheets-and-pinouts.md)), $R_{DS}$ = 0.2 Ω for the two DRV8874 FETs in the path, $L_M \approx 2$ mH (an **estimate** — exercise 02.03-E2 measures it):

$$\tau_e = \frac{2\ \text{mH}}{3.2\ \Omega} = 0.63\ \text{ms}$$

Compare that with the PWM period. The peak-to-peak current ripple in drive/brake is approximately

$$\Delta I_{pp} \approx \frac{V_M \, d\,(1-d)}{L_M f}$$

| $f_{PWM}$ | Period | Period / $\tau_e$ | $\Delta I_{pp}$ at 50 % duty | Audible? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 kHz | 1000 µs | 1.6 | **1.44 A** (simulated), 1.5 A analytic | yes, a loud whine at the PWM frequency |
| 20 kHz | 50 µs | 0.08 | **0.075 A** | no, above hearing |
| 100 kHz | 10 µs | 0.016 | 0.015 A | no, but switching losses ×5 |

1.44 A of ripple on a motor whose *mean* current is 0.1 A means the current is swinging between roughly −0.6 A and +0.8 A every millisecond: torque pulses, extra $I^2R$ heating in the winding for no useful work, and audible noise. That's why `config.PWM_FREQ_HZ = 20_000`. The upper bound comes from the driver's switching losses (Level 4) and its 100 kHz recommended maximum.

### Level 3 — Decay mode decides your duty-to-speed curve

Run `motor_driver_lab.py --section pwm`. It finds the free-running speed where the mean motor current equals the friction current, for each duty, mode and frequency:

```text
    duty    freq   mode     speed ideal d*V/k  I mean ripple pp
     0.1   20000  brake      90/s        90/s   0.100     0.027
     0.3   20000  brake     337/s       337/s   0.100     0.063
     0.5   20000  brake     584/s       584/s   0.100     0.075
     0.8   20000  brake     954/s       954/s   0.100     0.048
     0.1   20000  coast       0/s        90/s   0.003     0.030
     0.3   20000  coast       0/s       337/s   0.025     0.089
     0.5   20000  coast       0/s       584/s   0.068     0.147
     0.8   20000  coast     670/s       954/s   0.100     0.103
```

**Drive/brake tracks the ideal line exactly.** The average voltage applied to the motor is $d \cdot V_M$, because during the off time the terminals are shorted (0 V). Speed is linear in duty all the way down to 10 %.

**Drive/coast is a disaster at 20 kHz.** During the off time the motor sees $-(V_M + 2V_{SD})$ until its current reaches zero, and then nothing at all. The current reaches zero almost immediately at 20 kHz, so the motor spends most of each period disconnected: the effective average voltage is far below $d\,V_M$, and below 80 % duty the wheel doesn't turn at all in this model. On a real robot you see it as a **deadband** — karmel's `duty_deadband: 0.12` in `karmel.yaml` is the residue of friction alone, because the course firmware defaults to slow decay.

This is the single most consequential line in `motors.py`:

```python
motors = DriveMotors(decay="slow")      # drive/brake. "fast" = drive/coast
```

| | drive/brake (slow decay) | drive/coast (fast decay) |
|---|---|---|
| Speed vs duty | linear | strongly non-linear, huge deadband |
| Current ripple | small | smaller at low duty, but discontinuous |
| Low-speed control | good | poor — a PID has to hunt across the deadband |
| Behavior at duty = 0 | motor is braked | motor freewheels |
| Energy | the motor's energy is dumped in its own winding | returned to the supply |
| Use it when | you want controllable speed (karmel, always) | you want a gentle stop, or a stepper with current chopping |

**Deadband matters more than it looks.** Below `duty_deadband` a commanded velocity produces no motion at all; the integral term of the velocity PID ([08.05](../08-control/08.05-integral-control.md)) winds up until the robot jumps. `motors.compensate_deadband()` maps 0…1 onto deadband…1 so that a small command still moves the wheel.

### Level 4 — Losses and heat

Three loss terms, all in `driver_losses()`:

$$P = \underbrace{I^2 R_{DS(on)}}_{\text{conduction}} + \underbrace{\tfrac12 V_M I (t_r + t_f) f}_{\text{switching}} + \underbrace{2 V_{SD} I \, t_{dead} f}_{\text{dead time}}$$

```text
    I       f  cond W   sw W dead W  total  Tj JEDEC  Tj 70C/W   (TSD = shuts down, >= 160 C)
 0.50   20000   0.050  0.018  0.002  0.070       33C       35C
 2.10   20000   0.882  0.076  0.008  0.965       71C      121C
 2.10  100000   0.882  0.378  0.038  1.298       84C      152C
 2.95   20000   1.741  0.106  0.011  1.857      121C      TSD
```

Read three things out of that table:

1. **Conduction dominates at robot currents.** At 2.1 A and 20 kHz, switching is 8 % of the total. Raising the PWM to 100 kHz adds 34 % more heat for nothing.
2. **The thermal resistance is the whole game.** $T_J = T_A + P\,R_{\theta JA}$. TI's 36 °C/W is measured on a JEDEC test board with a large copper pour. A 0.6″ × 0.7″ Pololu carrier on a plastic chassis is much worse — 70 °C/W is a realistic **estimate** — and the same 2.1 A that gives a comfortable 71 °C on paper gives 121 °C in reality.
3. **`junction_temp()` iterates.** $R_{DS(on)}$ rises about 0.4 %/°C, which makes more heat, which raises $R_{DS(on)}$… At 2.95 A on a small carrier there is no fixed point: the model runs away and the real chip hits its 160 °C thermal shutdown, turns off, cools, and turns back on. **A motor that stutters rhythmically under load after 30 seconds is a thermal shutdown, not a software bug.**

Pololu rates the carrier at **2.1 A continuous** for exactly this reason, although the chip's peak rating is 6 A.

### Level 5 — Current regulation and IPROPI

The DRV8874 mirrors a fraction of its output current out of the IPROPI pin: $A_{IPROPI}$ = **450 µA/A** (typ, ±5.5 % between 2 A and 4 A). That current flows through a resistor to ground; the resulting voltage is both your measurement and, compared against VREF, the chip's own current limit:

$$I_{TRIP} \cdot A_{IPROPI} = \frac{V_{VREF}}{R_{IPROPI}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_{TRIP} = \frac{V_{VREF}}{R_{IPROPI} \cdot A_{IPROPI}}$$

**Example (karmel).** The Pololu carrier has $R_{IPROPI}$ = 2.49 kΩ and ties VREF to SLEEP through 10 kΩ. karmel ties SLEEP to the Pico's 3V3:

$$I_{TRIP} = \frac{3.3}{2490 \times 450 \times 10^{-6}} = 2.95\ \text{A per motor}$$

With SLEEP at 5 V it would be 4.46 A (Pololu quotes ≈ 4.4 A). That single wire is the difference between a 7.57 A and an 18.5 A worst-case battery current ([02.02](02.02-power-budget.md)).

When the current hits $I_{TRIP}$, the chip chops: with IMODE pulled low (the carrier's default) it does **cycle-by-cycle current chopping** — it turns the drive off for the rest of the PWM period and lets the current recirculate. The motor doesn't stop, it just stops accelerating. This is regulation, not a fault: `nFAULT` stays high.

**The measurement side.** The same node gives $450\ \mu\text{A/A} \times 2490\ \Omega$ = **1.121 V/A** (Pololu says "approximately 1.1 V/A"). At the 2.95 A trip point that is 3.31 V — right at the Pico's ADC full scale, which is convenient and dangerous. Run `motor_driver_lab.py --section sense`:

```text
design                                                         V/A pin  I_trip pin@trip  pin@6A   fc Hz ADC safe limit kept
A: SLEEP=3.3 V (karmel), 10k series + BAT54S clamp + 10 nF       1.121   2.95A    3.30V   3.30V    1592      yes        yes
B: naive, SLEEP=5 V straight into ADC                            1.121   4.46A    5.00V   5.00V     inf       NO        yes
C: SLEEP=5 V, 47k/68k divider + 1k series + clamp + 100 nF       0.649   4.56A    2.96V   2.96V      55      yes        yes
D: SLEEP=5 V, 1k/2k 'normal' divider (loads CS!)                 0.408   8.17A    3.33V   2.45V    9549      yes         NO
```

Four rules come straight out of that table:

- **A** works because the current limit itself caps the CS voltage at $V_{REF}$ = 3.3 V. Resolution: 1391 ADC counts per amp on the RP2350's 12-bit ADC, **0.72 mA per count**. The 10 kΩ series resistor plus a BAT54S clamp limits a 12 V wiring fault to 0.84 mA into the 3.3 V rail; the 10 nF gives $f_c$ = 1.6 kHz, which averages the 20 kHz chopping without hiding a 10 ms stall event.
- **B** puts 5 V on a **GP26–GP29 ADC pin, which is not 5 V tolerant even when powered** (limit IOVDD + 0.5 V). It kills the pin. See [02.05](02.05-logic-levels-and-protection.md).
- **C** is the right way to divide: with a 115 kΩ divider the loading on the 2.49 kΩ sense resistor is small, so the trip point moves only from 4.46 A to 4.56 A (2 %).
- **D** is the trap. A 1 k/2 k divider is 3 kΩ *in parallel with* the carrier's 2.49 kΩ, so the effective $R_{IPROPI}$ drops to 1.36 kΩ and the trip point rises from 4.46 A to **8.17 A**. The scaling on the ADC still looks plausible. You have silently removed your current limit — and your battery's worst case doubles.

**Braking energy and bus pumping.** Braking from karmel's top speed, `--section brake`:

```text
4) Braking from 0.77 m/s: motor at 958 rad/s, back-EMF 9.3 V, kinetic energy 0.47 J
   brake (short) initial current 2.91 A per motor; reverse at full speed would need 6.66 A
   battery disconnected, 50 % of the energy returned into 470 uF: bus rises to 34.2 V
```

With the battery connected, the returned energy goes into the pack and nothing happens. With the battery **disconnected** (or a blown fuse, or a BMS that just opened) and only the 470 µF bulk capacitor to absorb it, $V = \sqrt{V_0^2 + 2E/C}$ pushes the rail to 34 V — under the DRV8874's 40 V absolute maximum, but not by much, and a bigger robot or a bigger capacitor-less bus exceeds it easily. **Never unplug the battery while the wheels are spinning.**

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Version-sensitive** (verified 2026-09 against TI DRV8874 datasheet SLVSF66A and the Pololu DRV8874 carrier page https://www.pololu.com/product/4035, which confirms 4.5–37 V, 2.1 A continuous, ≈ 4.4 A default limit at 5 V, ≈ 1.1 V/A on CS, the 2.49 kΩ resistor, VREF pulled to SLEEP through 10 kΩ, IMODE low and PMODE floating).
> Carrier revisions change the sense resistor and the defaults. Check the page for the board in your hand.
> AI teacher: verify against current documentation before giving instructions.

## Diagram

The bridge, with the current path in each state:

```text
  drive forward (IN1=1, IN2=0)          brake / slow decay (IN1=1, IN2=1)      coast / fast decay (0,0)
        VM                                     VM                                     VM
        │                                      │                                      │
    ┌───┴───┐   ┌───────┐               ┌──────┴┐   ┌───────┐               ┌──┬────┐ ┴ ┌────┬──┐
    │ HS1 ON│   │HS2 off│               │HS1 off│   │HS2 off│               │  ▼ D  │   │  ▼ D │   body diodes
    └───┬───┘   └───┬───┘               └───┬───┘   └───┬───┘               └──┴────┘   └────┴──┘
     OUT1─────M─────OUT2                 OUT1─────M─────OUT2                 OUT1─────M─────OUT2
    ┌───┴───┐   ┌───┴───┐               ┌───┴───┐   ┌───┴───┐               ┌───┴───┐   ┌───┴───┐
    │LS1 off│   │ LS2 ON│               │ LS1 ON│   │ LS2 ON│               │LS1 off│   │LS2 off│
    └───┬───┘   └───┬───┘               └───┬───┘   └───┬───┘               └───┬───┘   └───┬───┘
       GND ────────GND                     GND ────────GND                     GND ────────GND
    i: VM → M → GND                     i: M → LS2 → GND → LS1 → M         i: M → diode → VM (!)
    loop voltage: VM − E                loop voltage: −E  (slow)           loop voltage: −(VM + 2·Vsd)  (fast)
```

karmel's current-sense network (design A), one per motor:

```text
  DRV8874 carrier                                       Raspberry Pi Pico 2
  ┌──────────────────┐                                  ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ CS (IPROPI)  ●───┼──── 10 kΩ ────┬──────────────────┼─● GP27 (ADC1, pin 32) │
  │  ↑ 450 µA/A      │               │                  │                       │
  │  └─ 2.49 kΩ ─GND │           10 nF │             ┌──┼─● 3V3 (pin 36)        │
  │                  │               │ │   BAT54S ───┘  │                       │
  │ SLEEP  ●─────────┼───────────────┼─┼────────────────┼─● 3V3                 │
  │ VREF (10 kΩ ↑ to SLEEP, leave)   │ └── to GND ──────┼─● AGND (pin 33)       │
  └──────────────────┘              GND                 └───────────────────────┘
       I_TRIP = 3.3 / (2490 × 450µ) = 2.95 A      fc = 1/(2π·10k·10n) = 1.6 kHz
```

| From | To | Wire color (suggestion) | Voltage / signal | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carrier CS | 10 kΩ resistor | white | 0–3.3 V analog, 1.121 V/A | series resistor limits fault current to 0.84 mA at 12 V |
| 10 kΩ other end | Pico GP27 (pin 32) | white | 0–3.3 V analog | `config.MOTOR_LEFT_IPROPI_ADC = 27` |
| Same node | 10 nF to AGND | — | filter | $f_c$ = 1.6 kHz: averages 20 kHz chopping, keeps 10 ms events |
| Same node | BAT54S to 3V3 and GND | — | clamp | survives a slipped probe or a 12 V short |
| Carrier SLEEP | Pico 3V3 (pin 36) | red, thin | 3.3 V | wakes the driver **and** sets $I_{TRIP}$ = 2.95 A |
| Carrier PMODE | Pico 3V3 (pin 36) | red, thin | 3.3 V | IN/IN mode, latched at wake-up ([02.01](02.01-datasheets-and-pinouts.md)) |
| Carrier GND | Pico AGND (pin 33) | black, thin | 0 V | the ADC measures against *this* ground ([02.06](02.06-noise-grounding-emi.md)) |

## Code

[`02-robot-electronics/code/motor_driver_lab.py`](code/motor_driver_lab.py) models everything above. Run the whole thing, or one section:

```bash
python 02-robot-electronics/code/motor_driver_lab.py
python 02-robot-electronics/code/motor_driver_lab.py --section sense
python -m pytest 02-robot-electronics/code
```

The decay modes are one `if` inside the period integrator — the whole difference between a linear robot and a twitchy one:

```python
            if on:
                v = v_bus
            elif mode == "brake":
                v = 0.0                                  # both low sides on: terminals shorted
            else:                                        # coast: current returns through body diodes
                v = -(v_bus + 2 * V_SD) if i > 0 else e  # until it reaches zero, then terminals float
```

On the robot, read the current sense in MicroPython. Save this as `labs/firmware/pico/examples/08_current_sense.py` (it only needs `config.py` and `motors.py`, which you already have):

```python
# 08_current_sense.py - read the DRV8874's IPROPI output while the left motor ramps up.
# SAFETY: wheels in the air. cd labs/firmware/pico && mpremote mount . run examples/08_current_sense.py
import time

from machine import ADC, Pin

import config
from motors import Motor

VOLTS_PER_AMP = 1.121          # 450 uA/A x 2490 ohm (Pololu 4035); calibrate it in 02.03-E3

adc = ADC(Pin(config.MOTOR_LEFT_IPROPI_ADC))
motor = Motor(config.MOTOR_LEFT_IN1, config.MOTOR_LEFT_IN2, decay="slow")


def amps(samples=64):
    total = 0
    for _ in range(samples):
        total += adc.read_u16()
    return (total / samples) * 3.3 / 65535 / VOLTS_PER_AMP


try:
    print("duty,amps")
    for percent in range(0, 101, 10):
        motor.set_duty(percent / 100)
        time.sleep_ms(400)                 # let the speed settle
        print("%d,%.3f" % (percent, amps()))
finally:
    motor.brake()
    time.sleep_ms(300)
    motor.coast()
```

`read_u16()` returns the RP2350's 12-bit conversion scaled to 16 bits, so the real resolution is 0.72 mA per count at this gain — far better than you need.

## Exercise

### Exercise 02.03-E1 — Predict both decay modes `[predict]`

Hardware: none.

Before running anything, sketch (on paper, two lines on one axis) wheel speed versus duty from 0 to 1, for drive/brake and drive/coast at 20 kHz, and write down:

1. At which duty does each curve leave zero?
2. At 50 % duty, what is the ratio of the two speeds?
3. Which mode draws more mean current at 50 % duty, and why?

Then run `python 02-robot-electronics/code/motor_driver_lab.py --section pwm` and compare.

### Exercise 02.03-E2 — Measure the real duty-to-speed curve and the deadband `[hardware]`

Hardware: `robot-base`.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** Robot on a stand, **wheels in the air**, hand on the battery switch. The wheel spins at up to full duty. Nothing loose near the wheels; no cables where a wheel can catch them ([SAFETY.md](../SAFETY.md) rules 1, 2, 7).

1. Edit `DriveMotors(decay="slow")` in a copy of `examples/02_motor_test.py` and sweep the duty from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05, reading wheel speed from the encoders (`examples/03_encoder_count.py` shows how).
2. Repeat with `decay="fast"`.
3. Plot both. Find the duty where each one first produces motion — that is your real deadband.
4. Optional, for $L_M$: set both inputs low (coast) from full speed and time how long the current takes to fall using `08_current_sense.py`; the decay is $\tau = L/(R + R_{DS})$ … but at 20 kHz you will need to drop to 1 kHz to see it. If your setup can't resolve it, keep $L_M$ = 2 mH marked as an estimate and say so.

No hardware? Use the simulated table from E1 and answer steps 3 and 4 from it, noting that the model's friction is a single constant.

### Exercise 02.03-E3 — Calibrate the current sense against the INA219 `[hardware]`

Hardware: `robot-base` (INA219 from [01.14](../01-first-robot/01.14-battery-monitoring.md), IPROPI wired as in the Diagram).

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** Wheels in the air. Do not hold the wheel still for more than 2–3 seconds at a time: a stalled motor at the 2.95 A limit puts ~1.7 W into the driver and 26 W into the winding.

Run `08_current_sense.py` and, at the same time, log the INA219's current. Drive one motor only, so the battery current is (almost) the motor current. Fit $I_{INA} = a \cdot V_{ADC} + b$ over the duty sweep. Report $a$ and compare it with the nominal 1/1.121 = 0.892 A/V.

No hardware? Compute what the ADC would read at 0.25 A, 1.0 A and at the trip point, and how many counts separate 1.00 A from 1.01 A.

### Exercise 02.03-E4 — Design a sense network for a 5 V SLEEP `[design]`

Hardware: none.

Someone hands you a robot whose DRV8874 carriers have SLEEP on 5 V (trip point 4.46 A) and wants the current on a Pico ADC pin. Using `SenseDesign` in `motor_driver_lab.py`:

1. Find a divider that keeps the ADC pin below 3.0 V at the trip point **and** moves $I_{TRIP}$ by less than 5 %.
2. Choose the series resistor and filter capacitor so a 12 V fault stays under 1 mA and $f_c$ is between 500 Hz and 3 kHz.
3. State the resulting volts-per-amp and the mA per ADC count.

### Exercise 02.03-E5 — Thermal budget for a ramp `[numerical]`

Hardware: none.

karmel drives up a 10° ramp. The extra torque needs about 1.4 A per motor continuously. Using `driver_losses()` and `junction_temp()`:

1. Power per driver at 20 kHz, and $T_J$ at $R_{\theta JA}$ = 36 and 70 °C/W, at 30 °C ambient (an Israeli room in September).
2. Repeat at 40 °C ambient.
3. At what continuous current does the 70 °C/W carrier reach 160 °C and shut down? Compare with Pololu's 2.1 A continuous rating.

### Exercise 02.03-E6 — The silent current limit `[debugging]`

Hardware: none.

A student reports: "I added a 1 k/2 k divider on CS so the ADC wouldn't saturate, and now my robot blows the 10 A fuse when both wheels stall." Explain, with numbers from `motor_driver_lab.py --section sense` and [02.02](02.02-power-budget.md), exactly what happened, and give the two-line fix.

## Expected result

- **02.03-E1:** drive/brake is a straight line from 0 to ~1230 rad/s, leaving zero at essentially any duty above friction (≈ 8 %); drive/coast stays at 0 up to about **0.75 duty** at 20 kHz in this model and only reaches 670 rad/s at 0.8. Ratio at 50 %: 584 : 0. Drive/brake draws more mean current (0.100 A vs 0.068 A), because the motor is actually doing work.
- **02.03-E2:** slow decay should be close to linear with a deadband of **0.08–0.15** (karmel's `duty_deadband: 0.12`); fast decay's deadband is far larger — typically **0.3–0.6** on a real motor (the model's 0.75 is pessimistic because it has no load inertia smoothing). Both curves flatten near full duty as back-EMF and supply sag catch up.
- **02.03-E3:** a slope within **±10 %** of 0.892 A/V, with an offset of a few tens of milliamps (the driver's own quiescent mirror current plus ADC offset). Larger disagreement usually means the INA219 is seeing the regulator's current too — drive only one motor and subtract the idle baseline. Numerical alternative: 0.25 A → 0.280 V → 348 counts; 1.00 A → 1.121 V → 1391 counts; 2.95 A → 3.31 V → clipped at full scale; 1.00 → 1.01 A is **14 counts**.
- **02.03-E4:** any divider with a total resistance ≳ 50 kΩ works; the lesson's design C (47 k/68 k, 1 k series, 100 nF) gives **0.649 V/A**, trip **4.56 A** (+2 %), **2.96 V** at the trip point, but $f_c$ = 55 Hz — too slow; 10 nF instead gives **553 Hz**, inside the required band. Fault current at 12 V through the divider plus the 1 k series resistor: **0.12 mA**. Resolution **805 counts/A** = 1.24 mA per count.
- **02.03-E5:** (1) 1.4 A, 20 kHz → **0.447 W**; $T_J$ = **47.4 °C** at 36 °C/W and **65.8 °C** at 70 °C/W. (2) At 40 °C ambient: **58.0 °C** and **77.0 °C**. (3) The 70 °C/W carrier reaches 160 °C at about **2.4 A** continuous (2.3 A → 146 °C, 2.4 A → 161 °C) — which is why Pololu's 2.1 A rating leaves margin, and why the 2.95 A current limit is a *peak*, not a duty cycle you can sustain.
- **02.03-E6:** the divider loads the 2.49 kΩ sense resistor down to 1.36 kΩ, so $I_{TRIP}$ = 3.3/(1360 × 450 µ) at 3.3 V SLEEP — or 8.17 A at 5 V. Both motors stalling now draw up to 2 × 8.2 A = 16.4 A plus the regulator, which is above the 10 A fuse. Fix: remove the divider (design A), or use a high-impedance divider (design C) and re-check `trip_a()`.

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: the motor stutters rhythmically under load after 20–60 seconds

1. **Touch the driver** (battery off first, then on — carefully; above 60 °C it will hurt). Hot? Thermal shutdown: the chip turns off at 160 °C and back on when it cools.
2. **Measure the current** with `08_current_sense.py` or the INA219. Above ~2 A continuous on a bare carrier, expect this.
3. **Reduce the load** (lighter robot, lower gear ratio, lower speed limit in `karmel.yaml`) or **improve the cooling** (a heat-sink pad to a metal chassis plate, airflow), or add a second driver in parallel for the same motor (TI's datasheet describes paralleling).
4. Distinguish it from **current regulation**, which is smooth and starts immediately at the trip point, not after a delay: the chip's `nFAULT` goes low for thermal shutdown, and stays high for current regulation.

### Symptom: the wheel doesn't move below ~40 % duty, and the velocity PID oscillates

1. Check the decay mode: `DriveMotors(decay=...)`. `"fast"` gives exactly this.
2. Check that **PMODE was high when the driver woke up**. Floating PMODE latches independent half-bridge mode at wake-up ([02.01](02.01-datasheets-and-pinouts.md)), in which IN/IN duty means something else entirely. Tie it to 3V3 and power-cycle the driver.
3. Measure the duty at the carrier's IN1 and IN2 pins with a meter (a DC meter averages PWM, so 50 % duty reads ≈ 1.65 V). If the pins look right and the output doesn't, continue with [02.09](02.09-electrical-debugging-method.md).

### Symptom: the current-sense reading is noisy, or reads full scale

1. **Full scale always?** You wired CS to a 5 V node, or the motor is at the current limit — check with the INA219.
2. **Noisy?** Is the filter capacitor fitted, and is its ground the *analog* ground (Pico pin 33), not a motor-return wire? Ground bounce shows up directly in an ADC reading ([02.06](02.06-noise-grounding-emi.md)).
3. **Reads a sensible value but 2× off?** Something is loading the 2.49 kΩ node: a divider, an oscilloscope probe (1 MΩ is fine, 50 Ω is not), or a second wire you forgot.

### Symptom: the driver dies when you disconnect the battery to "stop quickly"

That's bus pumping. The spinning motors dump their kinetic energy into a rail with nothing to absorb it. Stop with `motors.brake()` or a duty ramp instead, keep the bulk capacitor fitted, and treat "disconnect the battery" as an emergency-only action.

## Common mistakes

- **Using fast decay because "coast sounds gentler".** It is gentler, and it costs you the bottom half of your speed range. Brake between PWM pulses; coast only when you want the robot to roll.
- **Raising the PWM frequency to "reduce ripple".** At 20 kHz the ripple is already 0.075 A. Going to 100 kHz adds a third more heat and buys 0.06 A.
- **Reading the current from a divider on CS.** It moves the current limit, and the limit is protection you paid for.
- **Assuming the datasheet's thermal resistance.** 36 °C/W is a JEDEC test board. Your carrier is not one.
- **Treating the current limit as the continuous rating.** 2.95 A is what the chip allows in a pulse; 2.1 A is what the board can dissipate.
- **Forgetting that the driver's ground and the Pico's ground must be the same node for the logic thresholds and the ADC to mean anything.**
- **Unplugging the battery while the wheels turn.**

## Knowledge check

1. In the brake state, what voltage drives the circulating current, and in the coast state?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Brake: only the motor's own back-EMF $E = k\omega$ (a few volts), around a loop of $R_M + R_{DS}$ — so the current decays slowly. Coast: $V_M + 2V_{SD} \approx 13.8$ V opposing it, because the current has to push through two body diodes back into the supply — so it decays fast and reaches zero within a fraction of a PWM period.
   </details>

2. A motor has $R = 2\ \Omega$, $L = 1$ mH, and is driven from 12 V at 50 % duty in drive/brake. Compute $\tau_e$ and the peak-to-peak current ripple at 2 kHz and at 20 kHz.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $\tau_e = 1\ \text{mH}/2\ \Omega = 0.5$ ms. $\Delta I_{pp} \approx V d(1-d)/(Lf) = 12 \times 0.25/(10^{-3} f)$: **1.5 A** at 2 kHz, **0.15 A** at 20 kHz. Ten times the frequency, a tenth of the ripple.
   </details>

3. Predict: you change `decay="slow"` to `decay="fast"` and leave everything else alone. What happens to (a) the robot's top speed, (b) the deadband, (c) the velocity PID's integral term at low commanded speeds?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   (a) Barely changes — at high duty both modes apply nearly the full supply. (b) Grows a lot, from ~0.12 to several tenths. (c) At a low commanded speed the wheel doesn't move, the error never shrinks, and the integral winds up until the duty crosses the deadband and the robot lurches. Anti-windup hides it; it doesn't fix it.
   </details>

4. karmel's SLEEP pin is moved from 3.3 V to 5 V. Give the new trip current and the new worst-case battery current for both motors stalling (regulator at 1.68 A).
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $I_{TRIP} = 5.0/(2490 \times 450\ \mu) = 4.46$ A per motor. Both stalling: $2 \times 4.46 + 1.68 = 10.6$ A — above the 10 A fuse and above the Samsung 35E's 8 A continuous rating. The 3.3 V connection is a design decision, not an accident.
   </details>

5. Debugging: the driver runs at 2.1 A continuously and the chip reads 121 °C with an IR thermometer, but your calculation said 71 °C. What did the calculation get wrong, and does the error make the design safer or less safe?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   It used TI's JEDEC $R_{\theta JA}$ = 36 °C/W, measured on a large copper test board. A small carrier on plastic is closer to 70 °C/W. The calculation was **optimistic**: less safe. Always treat datasheet thermal resistance as a best case and measure.
   </details>

6. Why does a 1 k/2 k divider on the CS pin change the current limit, while a 47 k/68 k divider barely does?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The trip point is set by the voltage the mirror current develops across the resistance at the IPROPI node. The divider sits in parallel with the carrier's 2.49 kΩ. 3 kΩ in parallel gives 1.36 kΩ (a 45 % drop → trip rises 83 %); 115 kΩ in parallel gives 2.44 kΩ (a 2 % drop). Keep any divider ≥ 20× the sense resistor.
   </details>

7. Your robot brakes hard from full speed with the battery connected and nothing bad happens. The same brake with a blown fuse pushes the bus to 34 V. Where did the energy go in each case?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   With the battery connected: into the pack (it charges slightly) and into resistive losses; the bus barely moves because the pack is a huge, low-impedance sink. With the fuse blown: the only sink is the 470 µF bulk capacitor, and $V = \sqrt{V_0^2 + 2 \eta E/C}$ — 0.47 J at 50 % return into 470 µF takes 12.6 V to 34.2 V, close to the DRV8874's 40 V absolute maximum.
   </details>

8. You want smooth, silent motors *and* minimum driver heat. What PWM frequency do you choose, and what is the trade-off curve you are standing on?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Just above the audible band, ≈ 20 kHz. Below ~16 kHz you hear it and the ripple grows as $1/f$; above it, ripple keeps falling but switching and dead-time losses grow linearly with $f$ (0.018 W at 20 kHz vs 0.090 W at 100 kHz for 0.5 A). 20–25 kHz is the flat part of the curve.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Produce a **one-page driver characterisation** of your own robot and use it to fix one real behaviour.

1. Measure the duty-to-speed curve in both decay modes, with the wheels in the air *and* on the floor, and plot all four.
2. Calibrate the IPROPI reading against the INA219 and put your measured volts-per-amp into `08_current_sense.py`.
3. Measure the driver's case temperature with an IR thermometer (or a thermistor taped to it) after 60 s at three continuous currents, and fit your own $R_{\theta JA}$.
4. Use the measurements to pick a duty ramp and a speed limit for `karmel.yaml` that keep the driver below 100 °C on your floor.

**Acceptance criteria:** four plotted curves with the deadband marked on each; a measured volts-per-amp within 15 % of 1.121 and a stated reason for the difference; a measured $R_{\theta JA}$ with the ambient temperature recorded; an updated `max_linear_accel_m_s2` (or firmware ramp) that you can show removes a stutter, a brownout or a lurch you had before; and a one-paragraph justification of the PWM frequency and decay mode you settled on.

## Go deeper

- Texas Instruments, DRV8874 datasheet: https://www.ti.com/product/DRV8874 — read "Current Sense and Regulation" and the thermal section; every formula in this lesson comes from there.
- Pololu, DRV8874 motor driver carrier: https://www.pololu.com/product/4035 — the board-level numbers: 2.1 A continuous, ≈ 4.4 A limit at 5 V, ≈ 1.1 V/A on CS, the 2.49 kΩ resistor.
- Texas Instruments, "Understanding Motor Driver Current Ratings" (SLVA505): https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slva505a/slva505a.pdf — why the peak rating in the features box is not a current you can use.
- Pololu, Understanding Destructive LC Voltage Spikes: https://www.pololu.com/docs/0J16 — the companion problem to bus pumping.
- Microchip AN907, "Stepper Motor Fundamentals" — decay modes explained with waveforms: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/AppNotes/00907a.pdf
- Modern Robotics (Lynch & Park), free book PDF — section 8.9, "DC motors and gearing": https://hades.mech.northwestern.edu/images/7/7f/MR.pdf — where the motor constants used here come from; the video lectures are at https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/.
